segments.speaker: Rob
segments.say: so picture the early nineties. jensen, chris and curtis are squeezed into a diner in san jose, refilling the same coffee over and over because that's basically the only office they've got. and what they're asking is, why should only the big expensive machines get proper three d, put it in everybody's home computer and let the gamers foot the bill.

segments.speaker: Rob
segments.say: and honestly they almost didn't make it. the very first product was a disaster, they picked the wrong way of drawing graphics and practically every unit got sent back to them. the cash was running out. what saved them was being straight with sega, who handed over the money regardless, and then one last roll of the dice on the riva, which flew off the shelves.

segments.speaker: Rob
segments.say: then right at the end of the decade they bring out a new card and they don't just sell it, they invent a word for it, graphics processing unit. microsoft wants one inside its console and pays a couple hundred million before it's even made. forbes is putting them on a pedestal. most people would've been happy with that, a nice gaming business, job done.

segments.speaker: Rob
segments.say: but in two thousand and six they do something odd. think of your normal computer chip as four or five really quick people working down a to do list. a graphics card is a stadium full of slower people all doing a tiny bit each, together. cuda was the software that let any programmer, a chemist, a banker, boss that stadium around. and it cost you nothing.

segments.speaker: Rob
segments.say: now investors thought this was madness. you're making every chip pricier for teenagers who just want to play games, and you're burning something like five hundred million every year on it. the shares got cut in half during the financial crisis, sales were going sideways for what felt like forever, and you had hedge funds knocking on the door saying please stop. they didn't stop.

segments.speaker: Rob
segments.say: and then the researchers found it. first some people in california work out that neural nets train dozens of times quicker on these cards. then alex, a student in canada, plugs two gaming cards into his machine, enters the big picture recognition competition and just destroys everybody. after that everyone who wanted in had to use the same tools, right up to the people who made chat g p t.

segments.speaker: Rob
segments.say: this is what that gamble looks like as a picture. every bar is a year of sales going back to the turn of the century, and for ages you can barely see them, it's basically a flat line along the floor. and then look at the right hand side. that's it. whether it keeps going is panshul's problem, i'm just here to explain where it came from.

segments.speaker: Rob
segments.say: which gets you to the question of why them, why is everyone else measured against this company. and it isn't one advantage, it's really a stack of four, the silicon, the code, how it's all wired up, and who can actually get it manufactured. beating one isn't good enough. you'd need to win on every level simultaneously.

segments.speaker: Rob
segments.say: let's take the silicon first. if you just read the spec sheet you would buy the a m d one, it's got way more memory and it's less money. and yet in the data centre market they sell roughly a twelfth of what nvidia does, seventeen billion next to a hundred and ninety something. so the spec sheet clearly isn't what people are paying for.

segments.speaker: Rob
segments.say: second layer is the code. it's kind of like apple, right, they design the phone and the operating system as one thing so you never have to think about it. there are six million people writing for this platform and an enormous free toolbox that's been polished for nearly two decades. amd only turned up with their version in twenty sixteen. every fresh idea lands here first.

segments.speaker: Rob
segments.say: third one sounds boring but it isn't, it's the cabling. they can take seventy two processors in one cabinet and lash them together so that as far as the program's concerned it's a single enormous one. and to join cabinets together they bought an israeli outfit called mellanox, seven billion, and that bit of the business now brings in four times that every twelve months.

segments.speaker: Rob
segments.say: and the last layer, even if you came up with something brilliant tomorrow, who's going to make it for you. there is essentially one factory company on the planet, in taiwan, that can do the cutting edge stuff, and the step where it all gets packaged up is jammed. nvidia has already put its name down for more than half of that line and committed hundreds of billions.

segments.speaker: Rob
segments.say: you'd think someone with deep pockets would've closed the gap by now. google's had the best go, they have been making their own processors for more than a decade. amazon, meta, microsoft are all having a crack, and every one of them is still a customer. nine out of ten models get trained on this stuff. so you need a trillion dollar company and ten years free.

segments.speaker: Rob
segments.say: and i know what people think, isn't it all just the guy in the leather jacket. no. one of the other founders never left. the folks who look after sales and operations and research have been sat next to each other for fifteen, twenty years. the man who invented cuda is still in charge of it. employees voted it the top employer in the states.

segments.speaker: Rob
segments.say: ok so the elephant in the room, aren't we just back in the year two thousand. let me give you a sense of size. when america laid its motorways it cost about one percent of the economy a year. the internet cables, a bit more than that. the railways, just over two. this is heading for above three and a half, year after year.

segments.speaker: Rob
segments.say: where it stops looking like back then is price and usage. the darling of that era was cisco and people were paying a hundred and forty times the profits for it, this is nowhere near. and the cables they buried back then mostly sat there dark. try renting space in an american server hall today, there's hardly any left. plus the customers are swimming in cash.

segments.speaker: Rob
segments.say: and it's not hype, you can point at things. the people who used it to work out the shapes of basically all proteins got the chemistry nobel for it. there's a treatment for scarred lungs that got to human testing in about half the time it normally takes. swedish hospitals are picking up a fifth more tumours in mammograms while the radiologists are doing far less reading.

segments.speaker: Rob
segments.say: for ordinary workers, the studies are pretty clear. give it to someone who writes reports and they're done in a bit over half the time and the report's better. call centre people fix more issues, and the newest starters improve the most. we've seen this film before, cash machines were going to finish off branch staff and there ended up being more of them. it eats the chores.
